overview: Westpac Banking Corporation is one of Australia's 'Big Four' banks, founded in 1817 as the nation's first bank, serving approximately 13 million customers across Consumer, Business & Wealth, Institutional and New Zealand segments. It operates a full-service retail, business and institutional banking model with multi-brand consumer coverage in Australia (Westpac, St.George, BankSA, Bank of Melbourne) and a full banking and wealth franchise in New Zealand via Westpac New Zealand, Westpac Life and BT Funds Management (NZ). WBC.NZ is a secondary (foreign exempt) NZX listing of the same ordinary shares that trade primarily on the ASX as WBC.AX; it represents the whole Group's equity, not a standalone NZ entity — Westpac New Zealand Limited is a separately RBNZ/APRA-regulated, locally incorporated subsidiary consolidated into these Group results.

business_model.summary: Westpac earns the majority of income from net interest margin on a ~$890bn loan book (predominantly Australian residential mortgages) funded by ~$745bn of customer deposits and wholesale funding, supplemented by fee, markets and wealth income. Revenue is largely recurring/spread-based rather than transactional or project-based, though Institutional Markets and Treasury income introduce some volatility. FY2025 net operating income was A$22.4bn; H1 FY2026 was A$11.3bn (net interest income ~86% of the total, non-interest income ~14%).

revenue_streams.name: Business & Wealth (SME, commercial, agribusiness, Private Wealth, BT)
Institutional (Corporate & Institutional Banking, Global Transaction Services, Financial Markets)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - loan growth ~17%, higher Markets income

revenue_streams.name: New Zealand (consumer, business, institutional banking and wealth)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (retail/consumer mortgages and deposits) and B2B (SME, commercial, agribusiness, large corporate and institutional clients, government)
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly Australia (Australian housing loans ~$517.7bn of ~$890bn gross loans at Mar-2026, i.e. >55% of the book), New Zealand as a distinct reporting segment, plus Institutional branches/subsidiaries in New York, London, Frankfurt, Singapore, and Westpac Pacific operations in Fiji and Papua New Guinea

main_competitors: ASB/Commonwealth Bank NZ, ANZ NZ, BNZ, Kiwibank (in New Zealand)
competitive_position.market_position: Second- or third-largest of Australia's Big Four by mortgage market share; consistently losing share to CBA over the past several years. Australia: ~21% household deposits, ~21% mortgages (per APRA Sep-2025), ~16% business lending. Independent March-2026 mortgage data shows Westpac at ~20.7% vs CBA ~25.4%, NAB ~14.1%, ANZ ~13.2% — Westpac has lost ~3.2 points of mortgage share since 2019, the worst of the majors. New Zealand: ~18% consumer lending, ~17% deposits, ~16% business lending (RBNZ, Sep-2025), behind ANZ NZ.

moat_factors.description: APRA authorisation, capital and liquidity requirements, and the systemic importance of the Big Four create very high barriers for new entrants in Australian banking; similarly RBNZ regulation protects the incumbent-dominated NZ market
~$1.17tn total assets and ~$745bn deposit base give Westpac wholesale funding, cost-of-capital and diversification advantages over regional/non-bank lenders
208-year heritage and four consumer brands (Westpac, St.George, BankSA, Bank of Melbourne) provide broad market coverage, though brand strength has not translated into market share gains versus CBA
Mortgage refinancing costs and transaction-account stickiness support customer retention, but rising broker penetration and digital comparison tools are eroding this advantage industry-wide
CET1 ratio of 12.4% (Mar-2026), well above the 11.25% target, plus a large franking credit balance give flexibility for buybacks and special returns

weaknesses: Persistent mortgage market-share losses to CBA over 7+ years, the worst trend among the majors
Cost-to-income ratio (53.1% FY25, ~51.7% 1H26 ex-notables) remains structurally above peer average; management targets 'below peer average' only by end-FY29
ROTE (11.0% FY25 ex-notables) still below the market leader (CBA), a gap the Chairman explicitly flagged as a priority to close
Legacy technology and product complexity (the rationale for the multi-year UNITE transformation) creates execution risk and elevated near-term costs

History of regulatory and conduct failures (2020 AUSTRAC AML/CTF penalty of A$1.3bn; multi-year APRA operational risk capital overlay only fully released October 2025) weighing on reputation and management bandwidth

growth_drivers: UNITE transformation program - consolidating products, processes and technology onto a single stack to cut structural costs and close the cost-to-income gap to peers; first large-scale migration (BT Panorama wealth platform) completed March 2026
BizEdge and Westpac One digital platforms - aimed at faster business lending decisions and improved institutional client experience/competitiveness
Business & Institutional lending momentum - Business lending +15-16% and Institutional loan growth +17% in FY25/1H26, diversified across agriculture, health, professional services
Growing proprietary mortgage origination - increasing the proportion of new home loans originated directly (vs broker channel) to defend margins
New Zealand segment recovery - FY25 NZ profit up 13% YoY on 300bps of RBNZ easing since mid-2024 and improving credit growth outlook (5.7% in 2025, 6.3% in 2026 forecast)
Capital return - ~$1.0bn remaining on the on-market share buyback as of the FY25 annual report, supported by a significant franking credit balance and CET1 well above target
Regional Australia expansion - new regional service centres, Community Banking Service, and a moratorium on regional branch closures through 2030 supporting franchise breadth
Sustainable finance - sustainable finance lending +37% and sustainable bond facilitation share +40% in FY25, positioning for the energy transition lending opportunity

business.description: Management explicitly flagged intensifying competition in mortgages and deposits in the Q3 FY26 update, with mortgage system growth expected to moderate into 4Q26; non-bank lenders and brokers continue to pressure returns
Westpac has lost the most mortgage share of any major bank since 2019 (down 3.2pp to ~20.7%), a structural competitive weakness versus CBA

Multi-year, multi-billion-dollar technology/process transformation (~$807m cumulative spend to Sep-25, ~40% of planned FY25-1H29 investment) with delivery, cost overrun and change-management risk; elevated expense growth already lifted FY25 cost-to-income to 53.1%
New CEO Anthony Miller took over 16 December 2024 (prior CEO Peter King retired); strategy reset still in its first years of execution

financial.description: Core NIM fell to 1.78% (1H26), down 4bps half-on-half, driven by competitive loan spreads in Australia; NIM is sensitive to further RBA/RBNZ rate moves and deposit mix shifts
Group raised ~$24bn of new long-term wholesale funding in FY26 to date; funding costs and market access are exposed to global credit conditions

Impairment charges rose to 10bps of average loans in 1H26 (from 4-6bps), with new portfolio overlays added for energy-intensive sectors amid a revised economic outlook and Middle East conflict-related energy price disruption

regulatory.description: CET1 must be maintained above the 11.25% target under normal conditions (12.4% at Mar-2026); further add-ons possible if governance or risk lapses recur, as occurred 2019-2025 with the operational risk capital overlay (fully released Oct-2025 after the multi-year CORE remediation program)

Westpac paid a record A$1.3bn AUSTRAC penalty in 2020 for AML/CTF breaches; scams and financial crime remain top-five strategic risks, with ongoing investment in fraud prevention (helped prevent $181m of losses in 1H26) amid tightening regulatory expectations

Westpac New Zealand Limited is separately regulated by the RBNZ (with its own capital, liquidity and disclosure regime) in addition to Group-level APRA oversight, adding regulatory complexity for the NZ segment specifically relevant to NZX-listed holders

Mandatory climate reporting begins next reporting cycle; new Climate Transition Plan and net-zero commitments create compliance and lending-policy obligations (e.g., zero thermal coal exposure target)

macro.description: Australian housing loans are ~55%+ of the gross loan book; the bank is heavily geared to Australian house prices, household leverage and mortgage serviceability, which are structurally undersupplied but rate- and policy-sensitive

NIM and NZ segment profitability are directly affected by the pace and direction of rate cuts; RBNZ delivered 300bps of easing since mid-2024, and further moves in either direction reprice margins with a lag

1H26 filing specifically cites the Middle East conflict disrupting energy supply chains and raising prices, flowing through to household and business customers, plus generic global trade-policy uncertainty as top risks

House prices and credit demand forecast to rise ~9% and ~6.5% respectively in 2026 in Australia amid structural under-supply — a tailwind for loan growth but a longer-term social/political risk factor

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian GDP growth expected to improve to 2.4% in 2026 on falling rates, rising real wages and a robust labour market, though productivity remains weak. Business credit demand expected to grow 7.2% in 2026. New Zealand's recovery has been slower than expected despite RBNZ easing, with credit growth forecast at 5.7% (2025) and 6.3% (2026). Global growth expected around 3% in both 2025 and 2026, with trade tensions and geopolitical risk (including the Middle East conflict cited in the May-2026 half-year report) as headwinds.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately cyclical - earnings tied to credit growth, impairment cycles and net interest margin, all of which move with the domestic rate and economic cycle; large, diversified balance sheet dampens volatility versus smaller lenders
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - net interest margin (1.89% in 1H26, down from 1.95% in 2H25) is directly affected by RBA/RBNZ policy rates, deposit repricing lags, and competitive pass-through of rate changes to mortgage pricing
key_input_costs: Wholesale funding costs (credit spreads, term funding markets)
Staff costs and enterprise bargaining outcomes
Credit impairment provisioning tied to economic scenarios

recent_developments.event: Q3 FY2026 trading update: unaudited net profit ex Notable Items of A$1.8bn (+2% vs 1H26 quarterly average); NIM steady at 1.89%; CET1 fell to 12.1% (from 12.4% at Mar-2026) as RWA grew to $465bn; management flagged intensifying mortgage/deposit competition and expected mortgage system growth to moderate in 4Q26

1H FY2026 results: statutory net profit $3.414bn (+3% YoY, -5% HoH); interim dividend 77cps fully franked; CET1 12.42%; cited Middle East conflict energy-price disruption and 'global unrest' as an active risk requiring higher provisions; completed sale/separation of RAMS mortgage portfolio (A$75m separation/transaction costs recognised as a Notable Item)

FY2025 annual report published; profit after tax down 1% to $6.9bn; ROTE 11.0% ex-notables; cost-to-income ratio rose to 53.1%; EPS broadly stable at 201.9cps aided ~3cps by buyback; final dividend 77cps taking FY25 total to $1.53, 75% payout ratio ex-notables; total shareholder return 29%, best of the major bank peers

APRA released the remaining $500 million operational risk capital overlay following completion of the multi-year Customer Outcomes and Risk Excellence (CORE) remediation program, closing out the legacy AUSTRAC-related capital add-on

One-year anniversary of Anthony Miller succeeding Peter King as CEO; first full year included a strategy reset around five priorities (Customer, People, Transformation, Risk, Performance) and launch/acceleration of the UNITE transformation program
Transitioned external auditor to KPMG after 55 years with PricewaterhouseCoopers

JPMorgan upgraded Westpac to Neutral from Underweight, raising price target to A$36.00 from A$30.80, citing resilient earnings and low impairment charges; broader analyst consensus (~14 analysts) remains net 'Sell'-leaning on valuation, with consensus targets in the A$33-35 range versus a share price that has run up strongly (TSR +29-31% over the past year, best of the majors)

guidance.as_of: Q3 FY2026 Trading Update (10 August 2026) and FY2025 Annual Report / Full Year Results Presentation
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (year ending 30 September 2026) and medium-term to FY2029

items.notes: FY25 cost-to-income ex-notables was 53.0%, 3.7ppts above the peer average as of 1H25; management has repeatedly reaffirmed this medium-term target rather than issuing near-term numeric guidance

items.metric: Return on tangible equity (ROTE, relative to peers)
items.notes: FY25 ROTE ex-notables was 11.0%, 1.5ppts below the peer average as of 1H25; explicitly reaffirmed in both the FY25 annual report and the 1H26 results as the medium-term financial ambition

items.target: ~$807m cumulative spend Oct-23 to Sep-25, representing ~40% of total planned investment through 1H29
items.notes: Program remains 'in progress' against an on-time/on-budget target; first large-scale migration (BT Panorama) completed March 2026 and migration of commercial banking customers to 'One Commercial Bank' underway

items.target: Operate with a buffer above the 11.25% target ratio in normal operating conditions
items.notes: 12.42% at Mar-2026 and 12.1% at Jun-2026 (Q3 update); Board has signalled willingness to deploy surplus capital (buyback, capital management) given the franking credit balance and buffer above target

items.target: ~$1.0bn remaining under the on-market share buyback (as at FY25 annual report)
items.notes: Buyback added ~3 cents to FY25 EPS; further capital return optionality flagged given surplus capital and franking balance, though no new buyback announced as of Q3 FY26 update

items.metric: FY2026 outlook - lending growth and margins
items.target: No explicit numeric revenue/profit guidance; qualitative outlook of moderating mortgage system growth and intensifying deposit/mortgage competition into 4Q26
items.notes: Q3 FY26 update flagged mortgage growth likely to be below system given a cautious initial response to heightened competition and recent government housing policy changes

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Anthony Miller has emphasized 'disciplined execution' and confidence in the strategy's momentum despite 'global unrest' (citing the Middle East conflict's impact on energy prices and flow-through to customers). He has reiterated that closing the cost-to-income and ROTE gaps to peer average by end-FY29 is the central financial ambition, underpinned by the UNITE transformation. The Board (Chairman Steven Gregg) has stated it is prudent to carry surplus capital in an uncertain operating environment while balancing transformation investment against capital returns, noting the company's 'significant franking credit balance' and remaining buyback capacity.

bull_case: Attractively capitalised at 12.4% CET1, well above the 11.25% target, with a large franking credit balance and buyback capacity supporting ongoing capital returns to shareholders

UNITE transformation program offers a credible multi-year path to closing the cost-to-income and ROTE gaps versus peers (explicit FY2029 targets), which would be a meaningful re-rating catalyst if delivered

Resolution of the multi-year APRA operational risk capital overlay (fully released October 2025) removes a longstanding regulatory overhang and signals successful completion of the CORE risk remediation program

Diversified, oligopolistic Big Four structure with high regulatory barriers to entry in both Australia and New Zealand provides a durable earnings base and pricing power even amid competitive pressure
Business and Institutional banking momentum (loan growth of 15-17%) and an improving New Zealand segment (profit +13% in FY25) are offsetting mortgage share losses and diversifying the earnings mix
bear_case: Structural loss of Australian mortgage market share to CBA (down ~3.2pp since 2019, worst of the majors) reflects a persistent competitive disadvantage that UNITE and BizEdge have yet to reverse

Cost-to-income ratio (53.1% FY25) and ROTE (11.0% ex-notables) remain below best-in-class peers, and management's own targets don't call for parity until FY2029 - a long runway with execution risk along the way

Heavy concentration in Australian residential mortgages (>55% of the loan book) leaves earnings highly exposed to a housing market correction, unemployment shock, or prolonged period of elevated rates

Analyst consensus is net cautious (average rating skewed toward 'Sell' among ~14 analysts, consensus price targets around A$33-35) even as the stock has re-rated strongly (TSR +29-31% over the past year), suggesting valuation has run ahead of fundamentals

History of costly conduct and regulatory failures (A$1.3bn AUSTRAC penalty in 2020, multi-year capital overlay) demonstrates ongoing execution and culture risk that could recur, and net interest margin is already compressing (core NIM down to 1.78% in 1H26) as competition intensifies into FY2026 guidance
